paras: Every executive program page is built out of the same six claims, and after you have read four of them you stop seeing the words. There is a cohort of experienced people from many countries. There is faculty who still work in the industries they teach. There is a format that fits around a career, usually online with two residencies a year. There is a capstone built on a real problem from your own organization. There is tuition, presented in instalments, and there is a line about the network. None of it is untrue. All of it is written to be read by somebody who has already decided.

The candidate who has not decided is reading for something else, and it is not on the page. A prerequisite tells you whether you are eligible; it says nothing about whether this is the year. The deferral clause tells you the school expects lives to move; it does not tell you what a year of waiting costs you. What every one of these pages leaves out is the only question the admissions interview will actually turn on, which is not why a program, but why this one and why now.

Admissions officers are unusually direct about this when they are asked. They shortlist on the written application and then spend thirty minutes trying to find out what changed. A candidate who says they want to grow and broaden their horizons has described every applicant in the pile and made the case for nobody. A candidate who names the thing that moved -- the year the company outgrew them, the decision they could not defend, the meeting they sat through without understanding half of it -- has answered a question the brochure never asks.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson from published executive program materials and admissions interviews

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: I am applying in order to close a gap I can already see.
I chose an online format so that I could keep running the company.
The residencies are one week each, so most participants keep working.

I moved two commitments so as not to lose those hours.

listenings.text: The answer we hear too often is that the candidate wants to grow and broaden their horizons, and I want to be fair about this: it is almost always sincere. The trouble is that it is true of every single person who applies, so it makes the case for nobody in particular. When we ask why now, we are not asking a polite version of why. We are asking what changed. Something moved in the last year or two, and if you cannot name it, the committee will assume that nothing did, and that you are applying because it seemed like the right stage of life. And let me say something about the people who have been thinking about this for years. Being on the fence is not a problem. Half the strongest candidates I have interviewed were on the fence for a long time. What matters is whether they can tell me what pushed them off it. The ones who cannot are usually the ones we do not shortlist.

The page says ten to fifteen hours a week, and that number is honest. What nobody tells you is which hours they are. They come out of the evening, and they come out of Sunday, and your family will notice before you do. I would still do it again, but I would have that conversation at home first instead of in month four. The residency weeks surprised me. I assumed they were the teaching, and they are not, because honestly you could do that part online. The residencies are where the cohort turns into a group of people you would actually call, and that is the part that is still there two years after the program ended. My one piece of advice is about the capstone. Choose the problem you are already avoiding at work. You are going to spend a year on it either way, so it may as well be the one that is costing you money.
